title: Network Intrusion Prevention
summary: Network intrusion prevention is the inline inspection and blocking of traffic that matches known attack patterns, malicious infrastructure, or anomalous protocol behaviour, usually delivered through a next-generation firewall, a dedicated prevention appliance, or a cloud-native inspection service. Unlike intrusion detection, which only alerts on a copy of the traffic, prevention sits in the path and can drop a session, reset a connection, or quarantine a source, which raises both its value and its risk. Detection content combines signature and protocol-anomaly rules for exploitation attempts and malware callbacks, reputation and threat-intelligence feeds for addresses and domains, transport fingerprinting that can distinguish suspicious clients even inside encryption, and behavioural thresholds for scanning, brute force, and tunnelling. Teams enable signature sets selectively, tune and suppress noise until a blocking policy is trustworthy, and frequently run in detect-only mode first to measure what a block would have broken. The control provides virtual patching for vulnerable public-facing services that cannot be fixed immediately, interrupts command-and-control over web protocols and DNS, cuts off large-scale exfiltration toward known or suspicious external services, and contains fast-moving ransomware by dropping the file-sharing and remote-service traffic it uses to spread laterally. Its limitations are equally concrete: encryption and evasion techniques such as fragmentation, encoding, and polymorphic payloads reduce inspection fidelity, traffic that stays inside an allowed cloud service is hard to distinguish from legitimate use, east-west blind spots and sensor placement gaps leave internal movement uninspected, capacity limits force bypass under load, and every false positive is an outage that erodes the organisation's willingness to keep the control in blocking mode.
objectives: Explain the operational difference between detection-only and inline prevention and when each posture is appropriate.
Tune signatures, suppressions, and thresholds until a blocking policy is safe to enforce in production.
Triage prevention alerts for exploitation attempts, beaconing, and tunnelling rather than closing them as noise.
Apply virtual patching to an exposed service while the underlying vulnerability remains unremediated.
Assess the fidelity limits created by encrypted traffic, evasion techniques, and permitted cloud services.
Plan fail-open and bypass behaviour so that an inspection outage does not become a business outage.
